Title: Bacterial Cellulose as Biofabricated Textile Material: Biotinkering and Trajectories of Textile Materialisation
Abstract: Bacterial cellulose (BC) is increasingly studied in material design and biodesign as a biofabricated material shaped through cultivation, harvesting, and processing. In fashion contexts, however, BC is often identified as a leather alternative, particularly in sheet form. While this framing has supported its integration into design practices, it constrains BC's textile potential. This paper investigates how BC becomes textile material through multiple materialisation trajectories rather than through a single substitute material form. The study is a comparative analysis of sixteen cases, framed by Material-Driven Design (MDD) approach. Fourteen external design and interdisciplinary cases provide the comparative basis, while two hands-on experiments by the authors, developed through Research through Design (RtD) and biotinkering, examine BC as a natural binder for textile waste and within a BC–alginate extrusion system for filaments. Through this analysis, six trajectories of textile materialisation are identified: sheet, fibre, filament, yarn, biocomposite textile, and textile coating. These trajectories are shaped by different relations between cultivation, processing, textile assembly, and surface treatment, showing that BC's textile potential does not reside in one stable form but emerges through how biological growth and material transformation are distributed across textile practices. The paper argues that BC should be understood as a process-based biofabricated textile material rather than a leather substitute, offering a more grounded basis for engaging with BC in textile design, biodesign, and emerging material practices.

Title: Beyond Softness: examining how vocabulary marginalises the material narrative of native British wool
Abstract: Softness has become the dominant metric through which wool is evaluated in knitwear design. This paper argues that such language privileges fibres associated with Merino and marginalises native British and regional wools with distinct breed-specific qualities. Drawing on practice-based research, material experiments with native British wool yarns, and literature on wool fibre and supply chains, we examine how existing terminology fails to support design engagement with these materials. In response, we propose a five-part framework, Place, People, Process, Properties and Practice, to support a more nuanced wool literacy. Developing richer vocabulary for native British wool is not simply a matter of education, but a requirement for more informed and sustainable textile design.

Title: Colour Without Extraction: Towards Ethical Pigments
Abstract: This paper investigates how recycled textile waste, reconstituted as particulate pigment, reshapes understandings of material intelligence in textile design, proposing a specifically chromatic account. Through iterative dyeing trials on cellulose substrates conducted within the Perpetual Pigments research initiative, the study examines what occurs when colour is treated as an active participant rather than a controllable output. Drawing on new materialist theory and circular economy frameworks, the paper argues that waste-derived pigments introduce relational dynamics that challenge industrial assumptions of chromatic stability and control. Despite growing interest in bio-colour, recycled pigment systems remain underexamined within design research. This paper responds to that gap and proposes the term ethical pigments to name colour systems in which the conditions for ethical production are made legible through the material encounter itself.

Title: Design Decisions as Leverage Points of Textile Production and Supply Chain Orientation: Case Textile Colouration
Authors: Hirviniemi, Helmiina; Salolainen, Maarit; Larsen, Astrid
Abstract: Textile design decisions, from fibres to finished fabrics, are often seen as matters of aesthetics and product functionality. However, these decisions also shape, among other aspects, production systems, supply chain structures, and the environmental impact of textile manufacturing. Textiles are constructed in complex production chains that transform fibres into yarns and ultimately into finished fabrics. At each stage, design and production choices influence not only the visual and technical properties of the final textile but also its ecological footprint and production system. This paper argues that more sustainable textile supply chains are achievable within existing technological capabilities if design and production decisions are reconsidered. Many alternative production methods already exist but remain underutilised because industrial practices are shaped by mass production and the demand for standardised material properties. For instance, colour can be introduced at multiple stages of the textile production process at the fibre, yarn, or fabric level. Yet contemporary industrial systems often prioritise dyeing yarn or fabric. While this approach offers flexibility for supply chains and enables rapidly changing colour palettes, it is also associated with significant environmental burdens. Drawing on preliminary insights from mapping current fabric colouration-oriented supply chains, examining heritage fibre-stage colouration practices, and analysing how historical industrial development has prioritised certain production methods over others, this paper highlights how textile design decisions function as leverage points within the supply chain. Anchored in transformation research theories, the paper emphasises that textile knowledge-informed design, combined with supply chain management research, is essential to challenge current practices and guide the industry toward more sustainable alternatives.

Title: Designing Garments as Processes: Material Transformation, Temporality, and Care in Contemporary Fashion Practice
Abstract: Recent discussions on sustainability in fashion have highlighted the limitations of approaches centred on material choices, technological innovation, recycling, and circular systems, which often fail to address the underlying issues of overproduction and overconsumption. In response, this paper proposes a shift from product-centred sustainability toward process-oriented approaches that engage with the temporal life of garments. The paper analyses a bachelor-level fashion design project as a case study of designing garments as processes. The project explores garment development through bio-based coatings, compost-induced degradation, cracking, repair, and material renewal. These processes introduce transformation, instability, and variability as intrinsic design conditions rather than as defects or after-use consequences. The garments retain conventional typologies, while their material properties, surfaces, and silhouettes change through coating, staining, perforation, reinforcement, and re-application. Bio-based coatings alter the visual appearance, stiffness, and drape of fabrics, allowing existing or discarded textiles to gain new structural and aesthetic qualities. Exposure to biological agents induces degradation that transforms both the visual expressiveness and structural stability of textiles, requiring reinforcement and repair to enable continued use. The paper reflects on repair, reuse, and prolonged use as practices shaped not only through the lens of sustainability but also by economic conditions and inherited material cultures. The study does not propose a scalable industrial solution, but positions the case as an experimental and critical design approach. It contributes to rethinking sustainability in fashion beyond material optimisation and technological innovation, highlighting temporality, care, and material transformation as central to shaping patterns of use and value.

Title: Designing with Drafts and Cross-Sections: Reflections on How Representations of Woven Structure Shape Design Practice
Abstract: The draft, a grid of black and white squares used to specify where a particular warp crosses over or under a weft in woven cloth, is a common representation used to design and describe woven structures. The squares in a draft directly, or with a few modifications, translate to manufacturing instructions, which makes the draft a common representation used in weaving design software. In this paper, we describe how using a different woven structure representation, a cross-section, in a design tool that foregrounds different concerns. Specifically, we describe and reflect on our motivation, design, and initial testing of an interactive cross-section design tool and share how it helped us appreciate how a cross-section representation gives “voice” to the material conditions of weaving at design time — color interaction, layer structure, and loom constraints — that the draft tends to leave less immediately legible. We share our experiences to provide inspiration for future design tools and to help those interested in documentation and sharing of their designs consider how representations shape attention to different facets of the weaving process.

Title: Designing with Evolutive Colors: A Proof of Concept for Bio-based Dye Integration in Textile Design Digital Workflow
Authors: Barbot, Clarisse; Fuzier, Camille; Loïc, Bertrand; Emile, De Visscher; Mavros, Panayotis
Abstract: Current industrial textile production relies on petrochemical dyes. This dependence has led to growing interest in bio-based alternatives, although their adoption remains constrained by technical and cultural factors. In particular, bio-based dyes do not meet typical industrial standards for stability, diversity of colour choices, and reproducibility. Textiles dyed with bio-based colourants tend to exhibit colour changes under light exposure. Current design software systems were built with the conventional expectation of stability of petrochemical dyes in mind, making them ill-adapted to bio-based dye behaviour and thus hampering their industrial adoption. To address this gap, we propose the prototype of a novel design software for textile designers, which integrates visualisation of light discoloration of bio-based dyes over time. This proof-of-concept software integrates the characteristics of materials inherently unstable to light in the design of a knitted jacquard. We argue that integrating the specificities of bio-based dyes into design tools could enable designers to transition toward more regenerative design approaches. Grounded in an understanding of the chemical behaviour of dye molecules over time and the translation of these dynamics into computational representations and textile structures, the software encourages broader reflection on the role of digital design tools in influencing designers’ choices. This work opens perspectives for the integration of bio-based active materials into contemporary design, production, and use cycles, by reframing instability and evolution as intrinsic properties of the material rather than limitations.

Title: Developing an Industrial Microbial Colour System through Textile Printing
Authors: Lloyd, Ruth; Taylor, Alice; Ajioka, James; Collet, Carole
Abstract: Emerging microbial colourants offer potential for more sustainable textile coloration, yet their integration into design and industrial production remains limited by the absence of systems that support their use. While existing biotechnology research has focused on colourant production and environmental performance, less attention has been given to how these materials can be applied within textile workflows. This paper demonstrates how microbial colour can be integrated into textile design through the development of reproducible protocols and a structured colour system. Drawing on practice-led doctoral research conducted in collaboration with the biotechnology company Colorifix, textile printing is used as a method to generate and organise knowledge of colour behaviour. Through systematic print testing, controlled colour mixing, and iterative design application, relationships between colourant, formulation, and process are defined and made reproducible. The resulting Colorifix Microbial Colour System (CMCS) translates microbial colour behaviour into a functional system linking perceptual colour selection to technical production data. Organised through compatibility, mixing relationships, and reproducible conditions, the system supports colour selection, combination, and application within textile design and manufacturing. The research demonstrates that the integration of bio-based colour technologies depends not only on material innovation, but on the development of systems that structure and stabilise material behaviour. It positions textile practice as a means of translating emerging materials into usable forms for industrial application.

Title: Evolutive textiles design with the variability of natural dyes: a color-driven approach of textile design
Abstract: In a context of over-standardized color production and stability-based evaluations of dyes, this article proposes a way to embrace and implement natural dyes’ temporal variabilities in evolutive textiles design and discusses how taking these into account modifies textile design practices. As a designer and a material scientist working with a dyer craftswoman, we present an adaptation of color characterisation methods and a chromo-chronological database, and how these tools result in a proof of concept of a tufted piece with pattern apparition, paving the way for a color-driven textile design.

Title: Explore It - A speculative approach investigating the material intelligence of casein for future textile materials
Authors: Harsaae, Malene Pilgaard; Johannesen, Ronni Anthony; Bang, Anne Louise; Hort, Tine; Mølbak, Hanne Thaarup; Maagaard, Katrin Meinert
Abstract: In the fashion and textile industries, materials are a prerequisite for the making of products. Extraction and processing of these materials have a huge negative impact on the environment and in addition they spark ethical and social considerations. This paper presents a project where cultural heritage and material knowledge is employed to explore if history and tradition can contribute to intelligently develop novel and flexible casein materials for the future with less damaging impact on the environment. Constituted by speculative design and a material-first perspective, the paper introduces a case of material exploration with casein, which is a milk protein. First and foremost, the research investigates if formaldehyde can be replaced with glycerine and thus offer a more sustainable material for textiles compared to the traditional production of casein-based materials. In an interdisciplinary setting between materials technology, design and biometric science within a clothing context, casein is used as an ingredient to develop and prototype from a material perspective, from a design perspective, and from a user perspective to explore to what extend it is possible to include casein as a constituent in a novel flexible material that can be used for contemporary clothing. The research points to promising material pathways that seem relevant to pursue and explore further for design and use, especially the use of casein for flexible textile-like materials and the combination with post-consumer textile waste. In that respect it opens for a discussion on ethical and social aspects of ownership and use of novel materials technology.

Title: From Textility to Embodied Experience: A Practice-Led Generative Approach to Textile ICH Engagement
Abstract: Engagement with intangible cultural heritage (ICH) is increasingly framed as experiential rather than representational. However, textile ICH—particularly structurally complex forms such as Miao Piling Embroidery—is still often presented through documentation and visual display, limiting access to its embodied, processual, and perceptual dimensions. This paper develops a situated, practice-led generative approach that explores how textility can be translated into generative and embodied experience. Using Miao Piling Embroidery as a case study, textility is defined here as a conceptual construct that synthesises material, making, structural, and cultural connotations, understood as a system of relations including unit formation, layering, and repetition. These relations are operationalised as generative parameters within a shared visual basis, which is subsequently developed into embodied spatial experience. Across two iterations of this system in varied exhibition contexts, the study examines how spatial conditions reshape embodied perception and produce distinct experiential modes. The paper contributes a situated, practice-led approach for translating textile ICH into generative and embodied experience, positioning textility and embodiment as design guides for structuring generative and spatial engagement.

Title: Hooked: Programmable, Capacitive Sensing through Crochet as a Medium for Garments with Tactile Interaction
Abstract: Soft capacitive sensing in wearable textiles has many promising applications such as health monitoring, rehabilitation, or intelligent sports garments requiring sensitivity and sensory stability. Existing approaches either rely on rigid or semi-rigid components that compromise conformability, or on conductive yarn arrangements whose sensing geometry is fixed by the textile structure and difficult to adapt at design time. Crochet is an additive, stitch-by-stitch construction process which offers a largely unexplored route to programmable sensing surfaces, in which electrode geometry, baseline capacitance, and sensing range can be tuned directly through fabrication. We present a means of programmable capacitive sensing through crochet, enabling simultaneous integration of sensing functionality and aesthetic design within an additive, stitch-by-stitch manufacturing process. The system detects three distinct interaction modalities, namely proximity, soft contact, and pressure, with capacitance values mapped linearly to the brightness of integrated LED strings, producing expressive, real-time visual feedback through closed-loop control. Deformable and conformable to curved surfaces, the sensor maintains consistent behavior across positions and environments through automated adaptive baseline calibration. To explore applied pressure quantification, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network was trained to predict pressure from raw capacitance data, achieving an accuracy of 87.1% on the test data. The approach is demonstrated through Hooked, a crocheted wearable garment that functions as a distributed, fully soft capacitive sensing system with integrated light feedback, deformable and conformable to curved body surfaces. Four patterns originally drawn by hand illustrate both sensing and personal aesthetic expression. Hooked sits at the intersection of hand craft, computational design, and tactile expression: crochet functions here as an additive manufacturing process with a social, participative dimension, while capacitive sensing transforms the resulting textile into an expressive, touch-responsive interface.

Title: Imagining Open-Source Ecosystems for Experimental Weaving: A View from the AdaCAD Project
Authors: Devendorf, Laura; Gelosi, Deanna; Sandry, Etta
Abstract: This paper describes and reflects on a series of activities, performed from 2024-present, that looked to grow an open-source ecosystem centered around [Anon. Software], a tool for what we began to call experimental weaving. We describe how we came to see experimental weaving as a term that can capture approaches and applications for weaving beyond common characterizations that center disciplinary affiliation or professional identity. We sketch the boundaries and sites of experimental weaving as it relates to our project and offer insights on common needs and challenges our project presented for these groups. We conclude by envisioning broader ecosystems for experimental weaving that can honor the specificity and diversity of practices that the term brings together.

Title: Including the Hybrids: The Thread Arrangement as a Lens for Manifesting Textile Designers' Agency
Abstract: Current textile classification systems often divide fabrics into mutually exclusive categories such as weaves, knits, and nonwovens. While useful for distinguishing basic structural differences between textiles, such taxonomies frequently fail to account for hybrid structures and may inadvertently discourage research into them. This paper proposes the notion of the "thread arrangement" as a conceptual lens to nuance such rigid classifications and to manifest the creative agency of the textile designer. By synthesising insights from textile design, creativity, and classification theory with potential-focused perspectives from textile archaeology, the term is developed as a meta-category that emphasizes the duality of the textile as both a finished result and its previous deliberate act of arranging. Through the reflective analysis of terminology developed in the author's practice-based doctoral research and different types of textile hybrids, the paper demonstrates how this lens makes structural transgressions visible and describeable. The findings suggest that shifting the focus from categorical definitions to structural potentials can allow for a more inclusive understanding of textile hybrids. The thread arrangement framework provides a space for reflective discovery, acknowledges textiles as open-ended systems of arranged threads, and reinforces the textile designer’s role as their hands-on creator.

Title: LOOMING between shaft looms and a TC2 Jacquard Loom - A Serendipitous Expedition with Live Weaving
Authors: Lin, Pei-Ying; McLean, Alex; Milne, Helen; Vorselen, Femke; Andersen, Kristina
Abstract: This paper describes an artistic exploration of the potential for more lively engagements with a TC2 digital Jacquard loom. We listened to the loom to enable control of every warp thread in real time, allowing live manipulation of the patterns. This exposed us to the cognitive challenge of designing live for 2 to the power of 1320 warp possibilities. To address this, we made a customised TC2 control software interface, LOOMIMG, that implements traditional shaft loom logic as a digital, interactive weaving draft. Our tests with two experienced weavers suggest that this facilitates not only a creative space that is workable and exploratory, but also access to traditional weaving knowledge built on the foundation of shaft looms. The interactive weaving draft also offers the versatility to emulate shaft looms with customised shaft numbers and sizes, tie-ups that can be modified on the fly, digitally controlled treadling, and the ability to work with algorithmic logic in a weaving draft. We propose a broader reconsideration of the capability of existing fabrication machines through the semantic space of textile practices, and consider how the ‘language’ of textile making might be transferable to digital craftsmanship.

Title: Material Impasse: Decentering Intentionality through Uncertainty in Textile Craft
Abstract: Recent developments in textiles — including hybrid practices and new material innovations — point to the emergence of new ways of doing, sensing and reflecting through textiles. However, the tools used to investigate these remain anchored in conventions, failing to align with new ways of working reflected by theoretical movements like new materialism. This paper challenges existing methodologies for investigating textile making through the concept of uncertainty. It asks how we can engage more deeply with textiles beyond pre-established frameworks by pushing the affordances of methodological thinking. Drawing on a two-day ethnographic study with textile designer Melissanthi Spei, the paper traces an emergent methodological pathway — from pre-planned mixed methods through a pivotal encounter with an unresolved artefact, to creative writing and blind drawing as modes of re-reading the making process. It concludes by reflecting on how notions of affective materiality, intuition and emplacedness surface from the maker-material relationship and offers practical orientations for researchers seeking to work with uncertainty in textile and craft research.

Title: Mechanically Recycling Metallicized Fabrics
Authors: Herron, Maya; Kohler, Magdalena; Nieri, Tommaso; Spinelli, Daniele; Canesi, Ilaria
Abstract: Electronic textiles (e-textiles) are a problematic technology when designing for sustainability as they combine two of the most polluting industries - textile and electronics. While ‘design for disassembly’ is frequently proposed as a sustainability strategy for the end-of-life of e-textile devices, what happens after components are separated and whether they can still function in new contexts has not been sufficiently addressed. Metallicized fabrics are commonly used in the e-textiles space when crafting/designing to provide conductivity for an array of applications, thus this study is focused on the post-disassembly potential and limitations of these materials. We apply recycling techniques from conventional textile recycling to produce needle-punched nonwoven fabrics. Through the characterization of the produced materials and the exploration of piezoresistive properties we advocate for a more nuanced understanding of post-disassembly reuse and for expanding sustainable design for e-textiles beyond ‘design for disassembly’.

Title: Opportunities and challenges of toolpath-based 3D printed textiles: insights from Digital Design and Craft course
Abstract: Advances in additive manufacturing (AM), particularly Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), have introduced new possibilities for textile and fashion design through toolpath-based fabrication. This paper examines the opportunities and challenges of 3D-printed textiles, drawing on insights from five iterations of a Digital Design and Craft course, in which 101 students designed and produced wearable artifacts using computational workflows. This paper examines students’ projects, analyzes application types, discusses assembly techniques and post-processing strategies, and highlights how traditional textile manufacturing inspires the toolpath structures. The paper further discusses the opportunities of 3D printed toolpath-based textiles, such as supporting sustainability and enhancing personalization through accessible, low-cost technologies. Challenges include differences in tactility relative to traditional textiles, printer build-size constraints that require assembly, and reliance on post-processing to achieve three-dimensional forms. By framing these findings within an educational context, this paper highlights both the creative potential and current barriers of 3D printed textiles and suggests directions for future research, tool development, and design pedagogy.

Title: Reya: Reuse Yarn. Product, Process and Practice
Abstract: Reya: Reuse Yarn is a practice-led research project that investigates scalable methods for reducing pre-consumer waste in commercial knitwear manufacturing. Positioned within a circular manufacturing framework, the study re-evaluates knit as product, process, and practice to generate new insights into sustainable production. The research addresses the environmental and economic impacts of deadstock yarn, particularly low-value synthetic blends that are typically discarded due to limitations in quantity, aesthetics, and material consistency. Drawing on interdisciplinary knowledge from knit and visual colour psychology, the project employs a Knit Thinking methodology, combining tacit material understanding with explicit technical knowledge through iterative, material-led enquiry. The research exploits optical colour mixing in knitted fabrics, where blended yarns and stitch structures create a perceptually unified colour rather than identifying individual colours in the blend of small, evenly distributed contiguous points of colour. This demonstrates minor colour inconsistency with yarn substitutions. A pilot study and two commercial trials demonstrated the viability of this approach. Findings reveal that optical mixing enables the effective use of small quantities of yarns while maintaining consistent garment aesthetics and handle. Consumer testing further indicates widespread acceptance of minor colour variation, challenging industry assumptions regarding the necessity of colour uniformity. The research concludes that integrating blended yarn techniques into existing manufacturing processes offers an immediately implementable, cost-neutral strategy for waste reduction. By reframing acceptable colour tolerance, Reya: Reuse Yarn proposes a shift in industry practice that supports circularity, reduces environmental impact, and aligns with emerging legislative pressures such as Extended Producer Responsibility.

Title: Shaped Circular Knitting for Zero Waste Design: A Material-Driven Approach To Knitted Textile-Forms
Abstract: While 3D knitting is proposed as part of a solution to the fashion industry's waste problem, circular knitting is primarily used in wasteful cut-and-sew manufacturing processes and is rarely explored for its shaping potential. Using material-driven design, this research investigates the dimensional and material properties of knit stitch patterns within defined rectangular artworks, enabling the shaping of circular knitted textiles for zero-waste design. To exemplify this approach, we developed a design method that addresses several aspects of the shaping process, highlighting the possibilities for zero-waste shaping and exploring potential applications. Finally, we discuss the implications, limitations, and opportunities of shape-change circular knitting for the future of sustainable textile design and manufacturing.

Title: Sketching Fast, Sketching Slow: Extending Sketchnoting Practices With E-Textiles
Authors: Blumenkranz, Anna; Scholz, Barbro; Posch, Irene; Fuchsberger, Verena
Abstract: As design researchers, we are often challenged to make sense of qualitative data without losing its nuances and situated character in the process. Sketchnoting is a widely used technique for transforming data into personal and memorable summaries. Typically practised with pen and paper, it involves a combination of drawings and text. However, what often remains underexplored is the formative role of materials in shaping sketchnoting practices, leaving open questions about the kinds of knowledge different materials enable to articulate. This paper explores e-textiles as a medium for sketchnoting, examining how their temporal, materially composite, interactive properties influence processes of data interpretation. Adopting a research-through-design approach, we conducted four interviews with e-textile practitioners and interpreted them in the form of embroidered, conductive, and sonic sketchnotes, resulting in an interactive e-textile tapestry. Reflecting on this process, we contribute insights on how the materiality of e-textiles shaped (1) the pace of our engagement with data, (2) how we attended to different kinds of data, (3) the cyclical encounters with data, and (4) the intentional and embodied engagement with data through sensory interaction. Synthesising these insights and drawing on textile thinking, we propose “slow sketchnoting” as a methodological expansion of sketchnoting practices. We argue that this approach supports a reflective, multidimensional, and embodied engagement with data, contributing to ongoing discussion of how knowledge production can be articulated in design research.

Title: Soft Shapeshifters: Thai Backstrap Weaving as embodied interaction and soft system
Abstract: By Bine Roth and Wuthigrai Si, Published on 09/15/26

Title: Soft Shaping: Zonal Elasticity in Layered Woven Textiles
Abstract: Body-shaping garments establish form through mechanical action at the textile-body interface: corsetry through rigid reinforcement and lacing, elastic shapewear through elastomeric recovery. This study shifts attention from how a textile acts on the body to how its form develops and is organised before application to the body. The Zonal Elasticity System (ZES) is a moisture-activated self-forming system based on differing moisture-responsive behaviour within bonded cotton-linen assemblies. Twenty-four specimens across three phases examined how grain orientation, cut topology, constraint geometry, bond routing, pre-stress, and interlayer coupling directed deformation towards a defined waist region. Connected cut units propagated deformation across the field, and bias orientation with rotating-cell geometry supported in-plane shear and diagonal extension. Boundary closure and interior bonds directed deformation towards the waist axis, while pre-stress altered the resting configuration and produced an observable restoring response. Measured across the waist axis, activated specimens narrowed to between 54 and 81 per cent of their original width. Six three-layer specimens extended the principles through the textile thickness. Together, the findings provide a geometric framework for directing moisture-activated self-forming behaviour in layered woven textiles.

Title: Strain-sensing Auxetic Knit with Embedded Elastomeric Optical Fibers
Abstract: This study presents the development and evaluation of a novel strain-sensing electronic textile that integrates elastomeric optical fiber within an auxetic knitted structure. Conventional wearable sensors often suffer from motion artifacts due to the mechanical mismatch between human-joint movements and the positive Poisson's ratio of standard fabrics. To address this, a log cabin knit pattern combining knit and purl stitches was designed to induce an out-of-plane buckling effect, resulting in a negative Poisson's ratio. A stretchable elastomeric optical fiber with a diameter of 1.2 mm was embedded within a 1×1 rib channel to ensure stable electromechanical coupling without hindering the flexibility of the fabric. Mechanical testing showed that the strongest auxetic behavior was achieved with a stitch density of 6 stitches per inch and a 15×15 unit-cell configuration, whereas optical characterization identified the SPI 7 and 20×20 configuration as providing the most stable and continuous optical response over the tested displacement range. Pilot demonstrations of respiration monitoring and elbow-joint motion tracking showed that the integrated textile could continuously detect physiological and biomechanical deformation under realistic conditions. The findings confirm that the fusion of auxetic structural mechanics with optical intensity modulation offers a robust, body-conformable platform for next-generation wearable health monitoring, sports science, and soft robotics.

Title: Textile as Ecological Index: Casting Domestic Food Waste into Wearable Biomaterial Media through a Domestic Biodesign Framework
Abstract: This paper introduces a domestic biodesign framework for transforming household food waste into wearable biomaterial textiles that function as ecological communication media. Through a practice-based case study, the MILES apron, it demonstrates how dehydrated kitchen residues embedded in an agar-based composite textile can materialise dietary and ecological patterns through sensory properties such as texture, colour variation, and material stratification. The paper contributes three advances. First, it proposes a six-stage design scaffold for domestic-scale biomaterial fabrication that integrates communicative intent, waste-stream analysis, material testing, and biosafety into a replicable process. Second, it develops the concept of biological constitution as a design lens for understanding how ecological information emerges through material formation rather than being digitally encoded or externally represented. Third, it demonstrates how food waste can be reframed as a generative textile resource, producing wearable artefacts that operate as embodied indices of consumption. Positioned within tangible media, biodesign, and textile systems research, the work extends Living Media Interfaces and embodied interaction into domestic contexts. It shows that everyday waste streams can be materially reconfigured into readable textile surfaces, enabling non-expert makers to engage with ecological data through making and wearing. The paper frames textile fabrication not as surface production, but as the construction of communicative ecological media.

Title: Textile Commons of Care: Intergenerational Mending and Temporalities
Abstract: Visible mending is increasingly recognized as both a functional and creative craft practice and a form of material intelligence, where knowledge emerges through tactile engagement. This paper adds an additional layer that visible mending in community, where the act of mending is also visible, functions as a materially grounded practice of ongoing care through which knowledge and learning are distributed across people, textiles, and time. Drawing on a multi‑sited qualitative study, including a nine‑month global mending cohort, a visible mending workshop, and interviews with experienced menders, the paper examines how care aesthetics helps clarify the social and epistemic dimensions of textile repair and its connection to concepts of aging. Framed through care aesthetics, the analysis shows the role of materials as active participants in aesthetic‑care relations through embodied engagement with aging textiles over time. Menders describe “listening” to worn garments, responding to the damage, and learning through reciprocal adjustment between hand, textile, and each other, forming a commons of care developed through a multi-modal approach. The findings further demonstrate how visible mending links textile and bodily aging as interconnected temporal processes, reframing aging as a shared, relational experience. Menders draw parallels between mended garments and their own shifting bodies, interpreting visible repair as an aesthetic and ethical stance that affirms change, endurance, and accumulated histories. By framing visible mending as a social textile, this paper expands understandings of care and textile knowledge to include embodied knowing, shared attentiveness, and the temporal agency of materials and bodies.

Title: Textile Digital Drape Definition - TD3: Comparing Digital to Physical Design Considerations
Authors: Kuijpers, Alexandra; Nachtigall, Troy; van Bommel, Maarten
Abstract: Fashion design is, by nature, a very hands-on activity in which the touch and feel of a textile are considered vital to the design of the garment. Yet when designers work with digital fashion design software, they rely on digital textile definitions that are visual instead of tangible textile swatches. In this research, we created a new Textile Digital Drape Definition (TD3) that is heavily informed by textile drape properties. We compared the TD3 to traditional tangible textile interaction, via an intense workshop examining eleven textile sample swatches. The digital drape of the TD3 follows standardized textile science drape methods, and it is created using the measured properties of the physical textile. The participants (N = 24), all digital fashion designers, undertook a three-phase workshop where they 1) observed the TD3 and indicated attributes and design considerations for each textile, 2) repeated the process after a tangible interaction, and 3) reflected on the visual TD3 as a tool for determining attributes and design considerations for digital textiles. The results show which textiles benefit the TD3 and when tangible interaction is needed to better understand, interpret, and refine design considerations. The TD3 treats drape as an entity that combines its visual and measured mechanical properties. The TD3 is relevant for researchers, educators, students, and practitioners in fashion and textile design who work with textiles in digital design software. The research introduces a digital textile definition that effectively informs design considerations in digital design with needed standardized implementation.

Title: The Impact of Differentiated Post-Consumer Textile Waste Sorting on the Homogeneity of Recycled Yarns
Abstract: Post-consumer textile waste (PCTW) is increasingly characterized by complex multi-fibre blends, posing significant challenges for fibre-to-fibre recycling. This study investigates the influence of sorting, cutting, and tearing processes on nep formation and the resulting yarn quality during mechanical recycling. A three-stage sorting approach based on fibre composition and stitch density was developed and combined with systematically varied cutting and tearing processes. The results show that both input material characteristics and recycling parameters affect nep formation. In particular, thermally melted cut edges from garments containing polyacrylonitrile were identified as a potential source of neps. The findings highlight the importance of differentiated sorting and process optimization for improving recycled fibre quality and supporting high-quality fibre-to-fibre recycling of PCTW.

Title: Threading the Line: Switchboard Labor, Bodily Knowledge, and the Textile Traditions of Telephone Operating
Abstract: This paper positions telephone switchboard operating as a textile tradition in the full disciplinary sense: a practice organized around embodied skill, the transmission of bodily knowledge through community, and the production of relational connection as material output. Drawing on feminist labor history, textile theory, and Daniela Rosner’s framework of critical fabulation, it argues that the systematic erasure of switchboard labor by electromechanical automation constitutes a form of textile loss: one structurally identical to the suppression of feminized craft work in computing history. The paper then presents the design logic of This Is Vera, Hold Please, a performance installation in development in which a dancer’s body, instrumented with electromyographic (EMG) and inertial sensors, physically reconstructs the gestural repertoire of exchange work. The installation is framed as a practice-based research method for recovering what written records cannot hold: the kinesthetic intelligence of a practice that lived in the hands.

Title: Three-dimensional transformable textiles woven with hygromorphic high-twist linen yarn
Abstract: Shape-changing textiles woven using high-twist yarns offer the potential of a diverse design space of three-dimensional morphologies without the need to cut the textile or to modify the loom. High-twist linen yarn has moisture-responsive – hygromorphic – properties, with the orientation of the transformation changing with yarn twist direction. Used to weave transformable textiles it offers an alternative to synthetic active yarns or non-textile actuators. The material intelligence of the high-twist linen yarn is non-linear, and S- and Z-twist yarns may be combined to increase the diversity of textile morphologies. Developed through practice-based research, a series of experiments have been woven to demonstrate the potential of this material. To facilitate understanding, and with potential as a design tool, a visual language of diagrams mapping the forces in the textiles has been developed and is demonstrated alongside the experiments. This foundational research offers a demonstration of the transformative potential of high-twist linen in woven textiles, aiming to raise awareness of this under-researched material.

Title: Towards self-powered woven triboelectric textiles using commercial yarns
Authors: De, Swarnalok; Mohan, Mithila; Iannacchero, Matteo; Vihmar, Marie; Vapaavuori, Jaana
Abstract: Electronic textiles (e-textiles) are emerging as promising next-generation sensors with applications in sport, healthcare, defense, and human-computer interactions. On one hand, their soft interface with skin provides comfortable user experience and offers the advantage of tailoring the sensors to adapt to different body types. On the other hand, their dependence on external power sources such as electrochemical batteries for prolonged monitoring of physiological cues compromises these inherent advantages by incorporating bulky, rigid, and non-biocompatible components into the textile designing. In this context, textile-based triboelectric nanogenerators (T-TENGs) are gaining attention due to their ability to act as self-powering sensors. However, most of the high-performance T-TENG designs utilize laboratory engineered yarns or functional polymers to fabricate the sensors. The complex nature of the material engineering of these designs is a hindrance in the scaling up and cost-effectiveness required for commercialization. In this work, we employed solely commercial off-the-shelf yarns for manufacturing our T-TENGs. We identified suitable yarn pairs, an appropriate weaving structure and a strategy for incorporating conductive yarns into the triboelectric layers to create a fully machinable double-layer T-TENG (DL-T-TENG). This DL-T-TENG provides stable voltage output for >20000 contact-separation cycles. Additionally, the peak-to-peak output voltage can reach as high as 143 V and the sensitivity of pressure detection 0.27 kPa-1. Finally, with our DL-T-TENGs we successfully demonstrated the possibility of harvesting and storing usable electrical energy by exerting a force approximately in the range of common biomechanical movements. Additionally, we showcased the possibility of sensing small biomechanical movements like a gentle touch using our DL-T-TENGs.

Title: Towards Textile Templating in Mycofabrication: Knitted Structures as Substrate and Scaffold
Authors: Kaiser, Romy; Elsacker, Elise; Robertson, Martyn; Bridgens, Ben; Scott, Jane
Abstract: This study investigates the potential of knitted textiles as both substrate and three-dimensional scaffold for mycofabrication, contributing to the development of textile templating approaches in biofabrication. While textiles are commonly used as reinforcement in mycelium-based composites, their role as active, designable interfaces for growth remains underexplored. Two experimental approaches using Ganoderma lucidum were conducted: seeding-based inoculation and liquid-state fermentation. The first evaluated fibre substrates (namely acrylic, wool, cotton, and linen) on mycelial colonisation. Cellulosic fibres, particularly cotton and linen, supported more integrated and extensive growth, while wool enabled limited surface expansion and acrylic showed minimal colonisation. Overall, low biomass shows that textiles alone are insufficient nutrient sources, though fibre type influences moisture behaviour. The second experiment examined fabrication potential using submerged three-dimensional knitted structures. Cotton scaffolds showed more uniform colonisation and increased structural stability, whereas wool exhibited negligible growth. Growth patterns consistently followed areas of liquid exposure, emphasising the role of moisture and nutrient distribution and presenting potential transfer into textile design applications. The findings indicate that textiles function more effectively as moisture-regulating interfaces and structural guides rather than sole substrates for Ganoderma lucidum. By linking textile design parameters to mycelial behaviour, this research creates a basis for further development and highlights how CNC knit technologies and textile design choices can expand opportunities in mycofabrication.

Title: WarpForm: An Accessible Loom Add-On for Weaving Non-Rectangular Textile-forms
Authors: Klop, Savanne; Carazo, Manuel; Voorwinden, Milou; McQuillan, Holly
Abstract: Textile-form Weaving, in which the fabric and form are created simultaneously on the loom, can support zero-waste, on-demand production of textile-based products. However, textile researchers and designers are limited in their ability to explore the full potential of Textile-form Weaving because most looms do not allow for all variables to be manipulated. In this paper, we present WarpForm, an accessible add-on for a standard hand-operated loom that opens up new possibilities for weavers. Specifically, through enabling the variable consumption of individual warp threads, WarpForm allows weavers to create 3D and non-rectangular forms directly on the loom. Through a description of the add-on, the weaving process, woven samples, and a demonstrator, this paper aims to provide textile researchers and designers with accessible knowledge and tools to uncover further potential in Textile-form Weaving, moving the textile industry towards more sustainable approaches.
